analysis.one_liner: Cuts mercury, smog, acid rain, and carbon pollution from power plants, closing the loophole that lets old plants keep polluting.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote; it sat in five House committees until the 107th Congress ended, despite 22 cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required every fossil-fuel power plant — including the roughly three-quarters of large old plants exempt from modern Clean Air Act standards — to meet strict limits on mercury, sulfur dioxide, and nitrogen oxides starting in 2005, and to comply with a carbon dioxide allowance system. It paired those mandates with help for the losers: $75 million a year for coal and oil workers displaced by plant closures, $75 million a year for hurt communities, property tax relief for towns that lose a plant, and research money for capturing carbon. The bill was referred to five committees and six subcommittees and never moved again.
analysis.who_benefits: People who breathe air downwind of coal and oil plants: the bill's own findings cite fine particle pollution linked to roughly 50,000 deaths a year, smog that worsens asthma, mercury that makes fish unsafe for pregnant women, and acid rain. Residents of plant-hosting towns also gain from disposal rules for mercury waste and tax-base grants if a plant closes.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Communities downwind of old coal plants

how_it_helps.text: Sets hard emission limits on mercury, sulfur dioxide, and nitrogen oxides for every generating unit 15 megawatts or larger, effective January 1, 2005, ending the 'grandfather' exemption under which 77 percent of the 1,000 largest emitting units faced much weaker standards [S2][S3].

Creates a carbon dioxide allowance system for plants over 50 megawatts, with quarterly public reporting of emissions and disclosure to residential customers of the pollution tied to their electricity [S2][S3].

Requires safe disposal of captured mercury and combustion wastes so hazards are not simply moved from air into ground water, and adds utility steam plants to the list of sources regulated for hazardous air pollutants [S2][S3].

Cushions the transition: $75 million a year through 2016 for coal and oil workers who lose their jobs, $75 million a year for affected communities, and grants covering up to half of lost property taxes for towns where a plant closes [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Owners of old coal- and oil-fired plants, who would have to install pollution controls, switch fuels, or shut down; the coal mining industry, which would see demand fall; and electricity customers, who would bear some of the cost through rates. The bill offsets part of this with worker, community, and property-tax assistance funded by taxpayers.
analysis.who_pays_short: Coal plant owners, coal miners, ratepayers

drawbacks.text: The mandates would raise the cost of generating electricity, and some of that cost would land on consumers through utility rates — the bill offers no direct ratepayer protection, only transition aid to coal workers and towns [S3].

The carbon cap is designed as a rate standard — a fixed tonnage pool divided by estimated total generation — so if electricity generation grows, total tons emitted could still rise even while every unit meets its benchmark [S3].

Allowances can be traded and carried over, letting some plants keep emitting above the standard by buying credits, and the bill only 'expresses the sense of Congress' that some monetary value from crediting emission cuts should flow back to customers — a nonbinding provision [S2][S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The health and environmental gains are large and concrete — the bill's findings tie current power plant pollution to tens of thousands of premature deaths a year, mercury contamination, and acid rain — and the drafters tried to blunt the biggest fair objection by funding retraining for coal workers and tax relief for plant towns. The main honest concerns are higher electricity prices and a carbon cap built as a rate benchmark that weakens as demand grows; a rate-based design is a genuine design weakness, not a fatal one, and the other pollutant limits are firm.

outcome.mechanism: Introduced in April 2001, the bill was split among five full committees and six subcommittees, none of which ever acted on it, and it died when the 107th Congress ended in January 2003.

narrative.text: Rep. Thomas Allen of Maine introduced the Clean Power Plant Act of 2001 on April 3, 2001, with 17 original cosponsors [S1][S3][S5].

The Speaker referred it to five committees at once — Energy and Commerce, Education and the Workforce, Financial Services, Transportation and Infrastructure, and Science — with portions parceled out to each [S5].
Between April and June 2001 it was passed down to six subcommittees, including Energy and Air Quality, which handles Clean Air Act legislation [S5].
No hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor action ever appears in the record; the bill's last action is the June 20, 2001 subcommittee referral, and the Congress ended January 3, 2003 [S5].
It finished with 22 cosponsors — 20 of 208 House Democrats, 1 of 223 House Republicans, and the chamber's 1 Independent [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Owners of old, lightly regulated coal- and oil-fired power plants and the coal mining industry came out ahead: they kept operating under the grandfathered standards the bill would have ended, with no new mercury, sulfur, nitrogen, or carbon limits and none of the compliance costs.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Old coal plant owners and the coal industry

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was nearly all Democratic — 20 of 208 House Democrats and 1 of 223 House Republicans signed on — and no vote was ever taken, so the partisan shape of any floor fight was never tested.

industries.industry: Owners of old coal- and oil-fired power plants
industries.note: The bill would have ended the grandfather loophole that lets 77 percent of the 1,000 largest emitting units avoid strict standards, forcing controls or retirement by 2005. Their compliance cost is the public health benefit, so their interest in stopping the bill ran directly against residents breathing the emissions.

Stricter limits and carbon allowances would cut coal consumption by power plants. The bill acknowledges the hit by funding $75 million a year in worker retraining and community aid, but the industry's core interest lay in the bill not passing.

industries.industry: Makers of pollution controls and cleaner generation technology
industries.note: The bill's findings tout modern combustion methods, scrubbers, renewables, and fuel cells as the compliance path, creating demand for that equipment. Their gain comes with cleaner air for the public.

A plant closure would erase a major slice of the property tax base — the bill targets towns where plants provide 10 percent or more of it — but grants covering up to half of the loss, plus community development money, soften the blow.
